voiceover.text: So, how do you choose a third condition? Try it now. Name one condition, other than heart disease and cancer, that you think matters in Australia. Then answer three questions without looking anything up. Is it becoming more or less common? Who does it affect most? And what would reduce it? Notice which question you couldn't answer. That gap is the whole lesson.

The syllabus lets you pick the third condition, so pick with four tests, in order. One, can you state a trend: rising, falling or flat? Two, can you name risk and protective factors with a mechanism, a reason each one changes the chance? Three, can you say where and for whom it's changing? And four, does it contrast with the other two? A condition that behaves just like heart disease gives you nothing to compare. They're the same kind of tests you used to choose a group. Choose for contrast, because comparison is what the long answers ask for.

scenes.title: the map: kills or disables, prevented or treated

voiceover.text: To see contrast, use a map with two axes. Up the side: does the condition mostly kill, or mostly disable? Across: have gains come mostly from prevention, or from detection and treatment? Heart disease sits top left. It kills, and prevention cut it. Cancer sits top right. It kills, and screening and treatment improved survival. Now three candidates. Mental health conditions sit near the bottom, with a large burden of illness but comparatively few deaths. Injury sits on the prevention side, because road deaths fell with laws and safer cars. It's the leading cause of death for young people, while falls hit older people hardest. And type 2 diabetes sits low and towards the middle, sharing every modifiable risk with heart disease. Any of these works, if you can fill the profile.

The profile has six rows. Mortality: is it a leading cause of death, and which way is it moving? Morbidity: how much illness and disability does it cause? Incidence: are new cases rising? Prevalence: how many people live with it? Then risk and protective factors, and where and for whom it's changing. Fill each in trend words, with no current figure needed. And two honesty rules. Say when a measure is uncertain. And separate a rise in the condition from a rise in the counting. Wider diagnostic rules, a new test, or less stigma all add recorded cases, with no change in health.

scenes.title: type 2 diabetes: what the deaths can't see

voiceover.text: Let's fill it for type 2 diabetes, where the body resists insulin or doesn't make enough, so blood glucose rises. Mortality first, and here's the trap. Diabetes is usually a contributing cause of death, not the main one, because people die of its complications, mostly heart and kidney disease. So death certificates understate it. Morbidity is large: vision loss, kidney failure, nerve damage and amputations, plus daily self-management. Now a surprise. The rate of new cases has fallen by almost half since 2000. Yet the number of people living with it keeps rising, because people live with it for decades. That's the bathtub again: the tap slows, but the drain is narrow, so the level climbs.

Row five. Every modifiable risk is shared with heart disease: overweight, inactivity and diet. The non-modifiable ones are age, family history and ethnic background. Protection is activity, diet quality, and early testing, so treatment starts before complications. Row six, where and for whom. It follows the income gradient, rises with remoteness, and is much higher, and earlier, for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Peoples. Why so uneven? The same low income that makes healthy food and exercise harder also makes medicines, monitoring and appointments harder, so one determinant sets both the chance of getting it and the chance of controlling it. So there are fewer new cases overall, but when it starts in younger adults, they live longer with it. That matters, because earlier onset means more years for complications to build.

Now compare all three on four axes, and each axis is a paragraph. Mortality against morbidity: heart disease and cancer kill, diabetes mostly disables. Prevention against treatment: heart disease gained most from prevention, cancer from treatment, and diabetes sits between. Age: all three rise with age, but diabetes often starts earlier. Shared risks: diabetes shares heart disease's list, so one prevention measure cuts all three. And the conditions aren't separate. Comorbidity means having more than one at once. Diabetes raises heart disease risk, chronic illness raises the risk of depression, and depression makes managing a chronic condition harder. Together, they're worse than the sum.
Two things to remember. Choose for contrast. And know what a measure can't see.

Two exam questions. First. Place chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, a lung disease caused mostly by smoking, and dementia on the two-axis map, and give one reason for each position. Pause here to answer.

COPD goes on the prevention side, leaning towards deaths. Its death rate is falling, decades after smoking fell. Dementia both kills and disables. It's now the leading cause of death, after years of disability and care, so a mid or upper height scores, if you say which part you used. Gains are small from either side, because there's no cure. The classic mistake is placing a condition without saying why.

scenes.title: attempt two (more diagnoses after a stigma campaign)

voiceover.text: Second. After a national campaign to reduce the stigma of mental illness, recorded diagnoses of depression among young people rise. A headline says young people's mental health is getting worse. Assess this claim. Pause here to answer.

The claim isn't supported yet. Less stigma means more young people seek help, so more cases get recorded. That's a rise in the counting, and it's good news for care. To know whether health actually changed, you'd need another measure, like a survey repeated with the same questions. The classic mistake is treating more help-seeking as bad news.

So choose for contrast, fill all six rows honestly, and compare on four axes. Now look behind all three conditions. Each one rises with age, and the population underneath them is changing shape. Is an ageing population a crisis, or a design problem?
